title: Belief, Practice and -ism
theme: The suffix -ism: beliefs, movements and habits of mind
objectives: I can explain what the suffix -ism adds to a base word and what -ist adds to name a person.
I can use words such as nationalism, imperialism, and despotism to describe how beliefs and power shape history.
I can use optimism, pessimism, and realism to describe how a person or a text looks at the world.
I can use plagiarism and journalism to talk about honest use of words and information.
rationale: The suffix -ism turns a stance, a system, or a habit into a named thing: nation becomes nationalism, real becomes realism. Grade 8 history, civics, and literature are full of these abstract nouns, so decoding the suffix gives students a way into a whole class of words. The ten words are chosen to show the suffix doing different jobs: naming political systems and ideas (nationalism, imperialism, despotism), naming attitudes and values (pacifism, materialism, optimism, pessimism), and naming ways of seeing, writing, and reporting (realism, journalism, plagiarism). Students practice with the matching -ist form for the person who holds or practices the idea. The unit builds on partisan, allegiance, and cogent from earlier units, because many -isms are what people give their allegiance to and argue about.

words.def: Strong pride in and loyalty to one's own country, sometimes placing it above all others.
words.ex: Nationalism can unite a crowd at a stadium, but it can also lead people to distrust their neighbors.
words.ex2: Historians study how nationalism shaped the way people spoke about their country in the 1800s.
words.nonExample: Cheering for your school's team is team spirit, not nationalism.

apps.academic: A historian asks whether nationalism in a source builds unity, excludes outsiders, or does both.
apps.spoken: There was a lot of nationalism in the stands during the World Cup.
apps.writing: Use nationalism for strong devotion to one's nation, and be clear whether you mean pride or an attitude of superiority.

cloze.s: The leader's speech stirred ___, urging citizens to put the interests of their country before every other concern.

cloze2.s: A fan wrapped in a flag at the stadium may feel ___, a deep pride in the whole country.

misuse.s: Nationalism is the belief that no country deserves any loyalty or pride.
misuse.why: Nationalism is strong loyalty to a nation, not a rejection of loyalty.

words.frame: Nationalism can bring people together by ___, but it can also ___.

words.def: A country's policy of gaining power by taking control of other lands or peoples.
words.ex: In their report, the students described how imperialism changed trade routes and borders around the world.
words.ex2: Cartoonists once used a giant hand grabbing a map to criticize imperialism.
words.nonExample: Two countries that sign a fair trade agreement as equals are not practicing imperialism.

apps.academic: Maps from the age of imperialism show how powerful countries drew new borders across other peoples' lands.
apps.spoken: That cartoon is a criticism of imperialism.
apps.writing: Use imperialism for the policy of controlling other lands, and name who gains and who loses.

cloze.s: The museum exhibit explained how ___ led powerful nations to claim territory far from their own borders.

cloze2.s: Critics accused the government of ___ when it sent troops to take control of a neighboring region's resources.

misuse.s: Imperialism means a small country governing itself without any outside control.
misuse.why: Imperialism is gaining control of other lands; self-rule is the opposite.

visual.alt: A map with a castle and arrows spreading outward.

words.def: The belief that war and violence are always wrong and that disputes should be settled peacefully.
words.ex: Her pacifism led her to refuse to join any group that trained for fighting.
words.ex2: The club's pacifism meant that it protested every war, no matter which side started it.
words.nonExample: Someone who defends others but hopes for peace is not necessarily following pacifism.

apps.academic: Pacifism has a long history in many cultures and religions, and it appears in debates about war and service.
apps.spoken: Her pacifism came from watching her grandfather's stories.
apps.writing: Use pacifism for the belief that violence is wrong, and use pacifist for the person who holds it.

cloze.s: Because of his ___, he refused to carry a weapon, even when others urged him to.

cloze2.s: A strong ___ can lead a person to settle disputes through talking, even when talking is difficult.

misuse.s: Pacifism is the belief that war is the best way to settle every disagreement.
misuse.why: Pacifism rejects war and violence; it does not endorse them.

visual.alt: A white dove above two people shaking hands.

words.frame: A pacifist would respond to conflict by ___.

words.def: The habit of valuing money and possessions more than other things, such as relationships or ideas.
words.ex: The film mocks materialism through a family that measures happiness by the size of its house.
words.ex2: Critics of materialism say that buying more things rarely brings lasting happiness.
words.nonExample: Enjoying a gift and then sharing it is not materialism.

apps.academic: In literature, a character's materialism is often shown through the objects he chooses to own or to show off.
apps.spoken: My grandmother says materialism makes people forget what matters.
apps.writing: Use materialism for the attitude that possessions matter most; show it with a behavior, not just a label.

cloze.s: The advertisement fed ___ by suggesting that a new phone would make every day happier.

cloze2.s: Her grandmother warned that ___ can leave people always wanting something more, no matter what they already own.

misuse.s: Materialism is the habit of giving away all your belongings and caring nothing for objects.
misuse.why: Materialism values possessions highly; giving everything away is the opposite.

visual.alt: Shopping bags beside a bag of money.

words.frame: Materialism leads people to ___ instead of ___.

words.def: A hopeful attitude that expects good things to happen or sees the best side of a situation.
words.ex: Her optimism kept the team cheerful even after three losses in a row.
words.ex2: The farmers' optimism grew as the first green shoots pushed through the dry ground.
words.nonExample: Expecting the worst before anything has happened is not optimism.

morph.note: Optim- is a stem meaning best; it does not stand alone as an English word.

apps.academic: A writer who shows optimism often gives a character a reason for hope, not just a cheerful voice.
apps.spoken: I'm full of optimism about the new schedule.
apps.writing: Use optimism for a hopeful outlook, and give the reason the person feels hopeful.

cloze.s: Despite the storm clouds, the coach showed ___ by predicting that the game would still be played.

cloze2.s: A teacher's ___ about a struggling student can inspire the student to try harder.

misuse.s: Her optimism was clear when she said nothing would ever go right, so why bother trying?
misuse.why: Optimism expects good results; saying nothing will go right is pessimism.

visual.alt: A smiling face in front of a rising sun.

words.def: A habit of expecting the worst or focusing on what might go wrong.
words.ex: His pessimism made him pack three umbrellas for a trip to the desert.
words.ex2: The report's pessimism about next year's harvest came from three seasons of poor rain.
words.nonExample: Making a backup plan because you care about the result is caution, not always pessimism.

morph.note: Pessim- is a stem meaning worst; it does not stand alone as an English word.

apps.academic: Authors use a pessimistic narrator to make readers question whether the problems are as big as they seem.
apps.spoken: That's pure pessimism; you don't know it will fail yet.
apps.writing: Use pessimism for an outlook that expects bad results, and note whether the evidence supports it.

cloze.s: The coach's ___ showed in her warning that the team would probably lose before the game even began.

cloze2.s: A little ___ can be useful, because it reminds you to prepare for what could go wrong.

misuse.s: Pessimism is the cheerful belief that everything will turn out perfectly.
misuse.why: Pessimism expects the worst; believing everything will turn out perfectly is optimism.

visual.alt: A worried face under a rain cloud.

words.def: A way of seeing or showing things as they truly are, without making them better or worse.
words.ex: The painter's realism was so careful that viewers could see every thread in the old coat.
words.ex2: Her realism helped her face the budget: she did not hope for a miracle, but counted the money she actually had.
words.nonExample: A story about dragons and wizards does not aim at realism.

apps.academic: A work of realism pays close attention to ordinary details, such as how people actually speak and what they actually eat.
apps.spoken: I need some realism here: we can't finish by Friday.
apps.writing: Use realism for a style or outlook that sticks to how things are, and name a detail that proves it.

cloze.s: The novel's ___ about life in a small factory town came from details such as cold coffee and tired feet.

cloze2.s: With his usual ___, the guide warned that the trail was longer and harder than the brochure promised.

misuse.s: Realism is the style of making everything look magical and impossible.
misuse.why: Realism shows things as they really are, not as magical or impossible.

visual.alt: A detailed painting beside a watching eye.

words.def: Copying another person's words or ideas and presenting them as your own.
words.ex: Handing in an essay copied from a website is plagiarism, even if you change a few words.
words.ex2: The newspaper fired the writer when an editor discovered plagiarism in three of his articles.
words.nonExample: Quoting a sentence, putting it in quotation marks, and naming its author is not plagiarism.

apps.academic: Every borrowed idea needs a citation so that your essay does not slide into plagiarism.
apps.spoken: I didn't mean to commit plagiarism; I forgot to put the quote in quotation marks.
apps.writing: Use plagiarism for passing off someone else's words or ideas as your own, and explain how to avoid it.

cloze.s: The teacher explained that ___ includes copying a friend's homework and turning it in under your own name.

cloze2.s: To avoid ___, the student put every borrowed sentence in quotation marks and listed the author.

misuse.s: She was praised for plagiarism because she wrote every sentence of her essay from her own ideas.
misuse.why: Plagiarism is copying; writing from your own ideas is original work.

visual.alt: Two identical pages, one marked as a copy.

words.def: Rule by one person who holds complete power and uses it without limits or fairness.
words.ex: The history unit contrasted democracy with despotism, in which a single ruler could ignore the people.
words.ex2: In the novel, the villagers lived under despotism until a council of citizens finally took control.
words.nonExample: A class that votes on its rules is the opposite of despotism.

apps.academic: A source describing despotism often reports that laws were changed at the ruler's will and that no one could object.
apps.spoken: That sounds like despotism, not a fair team.
apps.writing: Use despotism for rule with no limits; it is stronger than saying a leader is bossy.

cloze.s: Under ___, the king could change any law at will, and no one dared to question him.

cloze2.s: The citizens' protest against ___ demanded a voice in the decisions that affected them.

misuse.s: Despotism is a system in which every citizen shares power equally and votes on each law.
misuse.why: Despotism is rule by one person; shared power and voting is the opposite.

visual.alt: A crown beside a heavy chain.

words.def: The work of gathering, checking, and reporting news for the public.
words.ex: A student interested in journalism joined the school paper to practice interviewing and fact-checking.
words.ex2: Good journalism separates what is known from what is only rumored.
words.nonExample: A private diary is not journalism, because it is not written to inform the public.

segs.m: a daily record or news publication

apps.academic: Responsible journalism requires checking facts with more than one source before they are published.
apps.spoken: She wants to study journalism and report for a newspaper.
apps.writing: Use journalism for news reporting, and name the habits, such as checking sources, that make it trustworthy.

cloze.s: In her ___ class, she learned to check every fact with at least two sources before publishing.

cloze2.s: Investigative ___ requires patience, because reporters may spend months confirming a single claim.

misuse.s: Journalism is the art of making up stories and presenting them as facts.
misuse.why: Journalism reports checked facts; making up stories is the opposite.

passage.title: The Isms Wall
paras: Mr. Chen's eighth graders were building a hallway display called the Isms Wall, and each pair had to explain one word that ends in -ism. "The ending means a belief, an attitude, or a practice," Mr. Chen reminded them. "And a person who follows it often ends in -ist."

Ana and Luis took nationalism, strong pride in and loyalty to one's own nation. Luis pointed out that it can bring people together at a parade, or push them to look down on others. Next door, Priya and Sam had imperialism, the policy of one powerful country taking control of other lands, and they argued about how to show it fairly: a map with arrows, or a quotation from someone living under that rule.

Tomas and Keisha were assigned pacifism, the belief that war and violence are always wrong, and materialism, the habit of valuing possessions above everything else. "They don't seem related," Keisha said. "They are not," said Mr. Chen, "but each one is named for a belief or a habit of mind, which is exactly what -ism does."

At the next table, Dev was worried about despotism. His poster showed a throne, but he wanted readers to understand that despotism meant rule by one person with unlimited power, not just any bossy leader. Meanwhile Hana had optimism and pessimism on opposite sides of a poster, with realism in the middle, because a realist describes things as they are.

Mia was finishing the journalism poster. Her first draft included a paragraph copied from a website, and Mr. Chen noticed. "That is plagiarism," he said gently. "It means presenting someone else's words as your own. A journalist who did that could lose her job." Mia deleted the paragraph and wrote the definition in her own words, then added the website's name at the bottom as a source.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "nationalism" most nearly means
choices: the practice of controlling other lands
a ban on public parades
strong pride in and loyalty to one's own nation
the belief that war is always wrong
qs.why: The passage defines it as strong pride in and loyalty to one's own nation, and it adds how it can bring people together.

qs.q: Why does Mr. Chen say that pacifism and materialism are alike even though they "don't seem related"?
choices: They are both about money.
They are both opposed to war.
They both name a belief or habit of mind through the ending -ism.
They were both invented in the same century.
qs.why: He says each one is named for a belief or a habit of mind, which is what -ism does.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Mia's first draft included plagiarism?
choices: She had the topic of journalism.
Her draft included a paragraph copied from a website.
She finished her poster last.
She wrote the definition in her own words.
qs.why: Copying a paragraph and presenting it as her own is what Mr. Chen calls plagiarism.

qs.q: Why is Dev worried about his poster on despotism?
choices: He thinks a throne is too hard to draw.
He wants it to show rule with unlimited power, not just a bossy leader.
He thinks the word is spelled incorrectly.
He believes that despotism is a kind of journalism.
qs.why: Dev wants readers to understand that despotism means rule by one person with unlimited power.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: The ending -ism names beliefs, attitudes, and practices, and knowing it helps students understand many abstract words.
Every word that ends in -ism describes something harmful.
Posters are better than essays for teaching history.
Students should avoid group projects about difficult words.
qs.why: Mr. Chen's reminder and the many -ism words on the wall show that the ending names a belief, attitude, or practice.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that end in -ism, read a short narrative about a class building a display of -isms, practice the suffixes -ism, -ist, and -al, and write about an -ism in a text or in life. The unit's habit is to find the base, name what -ism adds, and then check the meaning in context.

notes.va.nationalism.n: Nationalism can be a positive pride or a harmful sense of superiority; keep both possibilities in view and use text evidence. Avoid current political examples that put students on the spot. Model the parts: national + -ism.
notes.va.imperialism.n: Imperialism is a country gaining power by controlling other lands or peoples. Use maps and cartoons, and ask 'who gains and who loses?' Keep the focus on the word and the idea, and let the history course supply specific cases. Link to the -al base: imperial + -ism.
notes.va.pacifism.n: Pacifism is a belief that war and violence are always wrong. Students may confuse it with passivity; ask what pacifists do (protest, negotiate, serve in other ways). The word is built on a base about peace-making, so no morph breakdown is shown.
notes.va.materialism.n: Materialism is valuing possessions over other things. The word also has a philosophy meaning (the idea that only physical things exist); this unit teaches only the everyday sense. Avoid shaming students for the things they own; focus on characters and ads.
notes.va.optimism.n: Optimism expects good things. Optim- comes from a stem meaning best; share it as a memory aid only if students are curious. Contrast with pessimism on a spectrum with realism in the middle. Ask students to supply a reason for hope, not just a cheerful voice.
notes.va.pessimism.n: Pessimism expects the worst. Pessim- comes from a stem meaning worst; share as a memory aid. Distinguish from realism: pessimism assumes bad outcomes whatever the evidence, while realism follows the evidence. Be careful not to label a student pessimistic personally.
notes.va.realism.n: Realism has two uses: a literary or artistic style that shows life as it is, and a practical outlook. Show both. Students may say 'realism' means 'real'; stress that it is a way of seeing or showing. Model real + -ism.
notes.va.plagiarism.n: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. Teach the practical antidotes: quotation marks, paraphrase plus citation, and naming sources. Remember that students may plagiarize by accident; be matter-of-fact and focus on correction. The base is rare, so decoding by parts is not offered.
notes.va.despotism.n: Despotism is rule by one person with total power. Model despot + -ism. Contrast with democracy, and have students find the word's near-synonyms (tyranny, dictatorship). Keep historical examples general unless the history course has covered them.
notes.va.journalism.n: Journalism is reporting news for the public. The key practices are checking facts, using more than one source, and separating fact from opinion. Link to corroborate and slant. Students may think anything online is journalism; discuss how to tell.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The word despotism has the base despot and the ending -ism. A despot is a ruler with total power, and -ism names a system or belief, so despotism is rule by one person with no limits. I check the sentence: the king could change any law and no one questioned him. That matches. The matching person word is despot, and the adjective is despotic.'
discuss: Which -ism word in this unit could be both helpful and harmful, depending on how it is used?
How does knowing the suffix -ism help you decide whether a word names a belief or a person?
misconceptions: Plagiarism only happens when you copy a whole essay.
Realism is the same as pessimism.
extend: Create your own Isms Wall entry: choose an -ism not in the unit (such as heroism or tourism), explain its base, and draw a poster.
Interview a family member about a time that optimism or realism helped them make a decision.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the -ism and -ist pairs within two days by asking students to turn three bases into -ism and -ist words, and at one week by using nationalism, imperialism, and despotism in a short history paragraph. The earlier words partisan, allegiance, and cogent return when students discuss why people hold an -ism and how to argue about it.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: nacionalismo, imperialismo, pacifismo, materialismo, optimismo, pesimismo, realismo, plagio, despotismo, periodismo.
Cognate flags: periodismo is marked false because the English base journal differs from the Spanish base periódico; confirm the other cognate flags.

Etymology: optim- (best) and pessim- (worst) are given as stems; the claim comes from standard references and should be confirmed. No morph breakdown is given for pacifism or plagiarism because their bases are not stable English words.
Sense boundaries: materialism and realism have philosophy or art senses that are mentioned only in teacher notes.
